title: Cyperus imbricatus: How to Spot and Control Shingle Flatsedge
metaTitle: Cyperus imbricatus in Rice: Shingle Flatsedge Guide
metaDescription: Cyperus imbricatus, called ballayang or obod obod, is a coarse sedge in lowland rice. Learn how to spot it and dig out clumps before they spread.
excerpt: Cyperus imbricatus, or shingle flatsedge, is a coarse, tufted sedge weed of irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. Farmers know it as ballayang, balabalongutan or obod obod. This page shows how to spot it by its stems and flower heads, and how to control it before it spreads.

heroImage.credit: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This damo is a sedge from the Cyperaceae family. Its English name is shingle flatsedge, and farmers know it as ballayang, balabalongutan or obod obod. Cyperus imbricatus grows in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields.

It is usually a perennial, though some plants live for one season only. It spreads mainly by seed, and sometimes by rhizomes, which are stems that creep under the soil. Its flower heads hold many long spikelets, so one plant can leave plenty of seed behind. A clump that survives the season can also sprout again with the next crop. That is why removing whole clumps, roots and all, works better than cutting. Start early, while the tufts are still small and easy to lift.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Cyperus imbricatus
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Like other sedges, it has a solid, triangular stem with no nodes. The plant looks coarse and tufted, and it grows upright. Its leaves stay shorter than the stem. At the top, it carries a compound, umbrella shaped flower head. This head starts out green when young and turns brown as it matures. Look closely and you will see many long spikelets packed in each head.

items: Coarse, upright tufts with many stems growing from one base.
Three sided stems that feel solid, with no joints along the length.
Leaves shorter than the stems, so the flower heads stand above the leaves.
A branched, umbrella shaped flower head, green when young and brown when mature.
Many long spikelets crowded in each flower cluster.

blocks.text:
Like most sedges, Cyperus imbricatus competes with palay for light, water and fertilizer. Its coarse tufts take up space between the rice hills, and its roots draw on the same nutrients your crop needs. Because it is usually a perennial, an old tuft can keep taking those resources crop after crop.

Its flower heads hold many long spikelets, so missed plants leave a lot of seed in your soil. That seed can also end up in harvested palay and lower the quality of seed you keep. Thick tufts give rats and insect pests a place to hide near the rice hills.

items: Dig out the whole tuft with its roots and any rhizomes, because a clump cut at the surface can regrow.
Remove plants while the flower heads are still green, before they turn brown and shed seed.
Clear tufts from bunds and canal edges, where perennial clumps can wait out the dry season.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Sedges

If water and weeding cannot hold Cyperus imbricatus down, choose an active ingredient that works on sedges at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Cyperus imbricatus Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before their flower clusters turn brown, since one clump drops a great deal of tiny seed.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [sedge weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Cyperus imbricatus?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Cyperus imbricatus

items.q: What do farmers call Cyperus imbricatus in the local language?
items.a: Farmers know it as ballayang, balabalongutan or obod obod. In English it goes by shingle flatsedge. The Latin word imbricatus means overlapping like roof tiles, which describes the tiny scales on each spikelet. It belongs to the sedge family, Cyperaceae, so it has a solid, three sided stem instead of the hollow stem of rice.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Prevention comes first, so use clean seed and keep the field level with steady water. Then dig out tufts by hand with their roots before the heads turn brown. Clean the bunds after harvest too. If you need a herbicide, choose one for sedges that fits the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why is it hard to get rid of?
items.a: It is usually a perennial, so a clump can survive from one crop to the next. Some plants also spread by rhizomes under the soil. On top of that, each flower head carries many long spikelets that drop seed. So you need to dig out whole clumps and weed before the heads turn brown.
